title: US civil rights: sit-ins to Selma (1960–1965)
summary: How sit-ins, Freedom Rides, Birmingham, the March on Washington and Selma pushed the federal government into the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965).

keyterms.definition: Protest in which activists occupy seats at a segregated facility, such as a lunch counter, and refuse to leave until served.
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, founded in April 1960 with Ella Baker's support to organise young activists.
Congress of Racial Equality (1942), which organised the 1961 Freedom Rides.
1961 interracial bus journeys through the South to test court rulings banning segregation in interstate travel facilities.
1963 SCLC campaign in Alabama whose televised police violence against child marchers built national support for legislation.
28 August 1963 demonstration of about 250,000 people for jobs and freedom, where King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
Law banning segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment, signed by Lyndon Johnson on 2 July 1964.
1964 Mississippi voter-registration campaign by mainly student volunteers; three workers were murdered in June.
1965 Alabama voting-rights campaign; the 'Bloody Sunday' attack on marchers on 7 March led to national outrage.
Law banning literacy tests and allowing federal registrars in areas with low Black registration; signed 6 August 1965.
Nation of Islam spokesman who criticised integration and non-violence; assassinated in February 1965.

questions.text: The 1960 sit-in movement began at a Woolworth's lunch counter in ___, North Carolina.
questions.explanation: Four students from North Carolina A&T began the protest on 1 February 1960; sit-ins spread to dozens of cities within weeks.

questions.prompt: Which organisation grew directly out of the 1960 sit-ins?
questions.explanation: Ella Baker encouraged students to form their own group in April 1960 rather than join the SCLC.

questions.statement: The Freedom Rides were organised by CORE to test desegregation of interstate bus facilities.
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court's Boynton v. Virginia (1960) ruling had banned segregation in interstate bus terminals, but it was ignored in the South.

questions.prompt: What happened to a Freedom Riders' bus at Anniston, Alabama, in May 1961?
options: It was firebombed by a white mob
It was escorted safely by the FBI
Its passengers were welcomed by the mayor
questions.explanation: The violence forced the Kennedy administration to intervene; the Interstate Commerce Commission later enforced desegregation.

questions.prompt: Why is the Albany Movement (1961–62) often seen as a setback?
options: Police chief Laurie Pritchett avoided public violence, denying the movement national attention
questions.explanation: Pritchett's mass arrests without visible brutality taught King that dramatic confrontation was needed to win national sympathy.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role in 1963.

pairs.right: Birmingham minister who invited the SCLC
Mississippi NAACP leader murdered in June

questions.explanation: Connor's use of dogs and fire hoses on children was broadcast across the world.

questions.text: While jailed in 1963 King wrote his 'Letter from ___ Jail'.
questions.explanation: The letter defended direct action against white moderates who urged patience.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
items: James Meredith enrols at the University of Mississippi
questions.explanation: February 1960, May 1961, October 1962, April–May 1963, August 1963.

questions.statement: President Kennedy announced plans for a major civil rights bill in June 1963, after Birmingham.
questions.explanation: His televised address of 11 June 1963 called civil rights a moral issue; the bill passed after his assassination.

questions.prompt: Why did the Birmingham 'Children's Crusade' prove so effective?
options: Images of police attacking children with dogs and hoses shocked national and world opinion
The children persuaded Bull Connor to resign immediately
It was ignored by the media
questions.explanation: The campaign exploited the media and the Cold War context, where US racism damaged America's image abroad.

questions.prompt: Which president signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
questions.explanation: Johnson used Kennedy's memory and his own Senate experience to overcome a long Southern filibuster.

questions.statement: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in employment as well as segregation in public places.
questions.explanation: Title VII outlawed employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin and created the EEOC.

questions.text: The 1964 voter-registration campaign in Mississippi was called Freedom ___.
questions.explanation: The murders of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner drew national attention, partly because two were white Northerners.

questions.prompt: What did the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party try to do in 1964?
options: Replace the all-white Mississippi delegation at the Democratic National Convention
questions.explanation: Fannie Lou Hamer's testimony was televised, but the MFDP was offered only two seats, disillusioning many SNCC activists.

questions.prompt: Match each law or amendment to what it did.

pairs.right: Banned poll taxes in federal elections
Suspended literacy tests and sent federal registrars

questions.explanation: Federal legislation came in stages, with voting rights last.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
questions.explanation: September 1963, July 1964, February 1965, March 1965, August 1965.

questions.prompt: Where did state troopers attack marchers on 'Bloody Sunday', 7 March 1965?
questions.explanation: John Lewis was among those beaten; the televised violence pushed Johnson to send a voting rights bill to Congress.

questions.text: The Voting Rights Act was signed in August ___.
questions.explanation: Black registration in Mississippi rose from about 7% to about 60% within a few years.

questions.statement: Malcolm X shared King's commitment to integration through non-violence throughout his career.
questions.explanation: As a Nation of Islam spokesman he rejected integration and defended self-defence; after leaving in 1964 he moved towards broader cooperation.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the historiographical shift in studying the civil rights movement?
options: Historians now stress local grassroots activists alongside national leaders like King
Historians now argue the movement achieved nothing
Historians agree the movement began in 1965
questions.explanation: 'Bottom-up' studies highlight figures such as Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer and local organising, not just King and Washington.
